items.title: RMIT builds dolphin-shaped minibot to skim oil spills

featured_image.name: Sneaker-sized 'Electronic Dolphin' robot could transform oil ...

items.description: Engineers at RMIT University in Australia have built a remote-controlled minibot shaped like a dolphin that skims oil from the surface of water using a filter inspired by the spiny structure of sea urchins. The proof-of-concept device, called the "Electronic Dolphin," is about the size of a sneaker and could offer a safer, more targeted way to respond to oil spills in sensitive environments.[1][2]

items.title: CSIRO and India complete world-first green steel trial using rice husk waste

featured_image.name: Australia-India partnership takes step closer to green steel ...

items.description:
Researchers from Australia and India have completed what they describe as a world-first commercial trial using agricultural waste to partially replace coal in steelmaking, offering a scalable pathway to cut emissions in one of the planet's most carbon-intensive industries.

The trial, announced on March 10 by CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, saw scientists blend rice husk pellets into gasifiers at a Jindal Steel facility in Odisha, India. Working alongside the Indian Institute of Science and RESCONS Solutions, a steel technology company incubated at IISc, the team substituted 5 and 10 percent of coal with locally sourced rice husk pellets while maintaining steady syngas production and no loss in operating performance.[1][2]

items.title: Scientists identify landing sites for China's first crewed moon mission

featured_image.name: China reveals how it plans to put astronauts on the moon by ...

items.description:
Chinese and international scientists have identified four potential landing sites in the volcanic Rimae Bode region on the moon's near side, advancing planning for what would be China's first crewed lunar mission before the end of the decade.

The findings, published March 9 in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Astronomy, present a detailed geological assessment of the equatorial region, which researchers describe as a "geological museum" combining high scientific value with safe conditions for astronaut access.[1][2]

items.title: UCL scientists reconstruct videos from mouse brain activity

featured_image.name: A new AI tool that can decode brain signals proves '95% accurate' on mice

items.description: Scientists at University College London have reconstructed 10-second video clips purely from the brain activity of mice, marking what researchers say is the first time natural movies have been successfully recovered from single-cell recordings in the visual cortex. The findings, published Monday in the journal eLife, could open new paths for understanding how the brain processes and distorts visual information.[1][2]

items.title: Apple now assembles 25% of iPhones in India

featured_image.name: Apple puts iPhone assembler Foxconn's India plant on notice ...

items.description: Apple assembled roughly 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53 percent jump from 36 million the year before, according to a Bloomberg report published Monday. The milestone means that about one in every four iPhones produced worldwide is now made in India, as the company accelerates efforts to diversify manufacturing away from China amid persistent U.S. tariff pressures.[1]

items.title: Oil surges to four-year high as Middle East war enters tenth day

featured_image.name: Oil and gas prices rise rapidly as Iran war escalates

items.description: The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, now in its tenth day, has effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, sent oil prices to their highest levels since the pandemic, and compounded an already dire humanitarian situation in Afghanistan — where a simultaneous border war with Pakistan and the halt of Iranian food exports are pushing millions closer to famine.

items.title: ALMA detects high methanol levels in interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS

featured_image.name: An interstellar comet packed with alcohol? What ALMA found in 3I/ATLAS

items.description:
Astronomers using one of the world's most powerful radio telescope arrays have discovered that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains extraordinary levels of methanol compared with hydrogen cyanide, a chemical fingerprint unlike nearly anything observed in comets born in our own solar system. The findings, announced by the ALMA Observatory on March 8, suggest the comet formed under conditions vastly different from those that shaped familiar solar system objects.[1]

The research team, led by Nathan Roth, a professor at American University, used ALMA's Atacama Compact Array in Chile to observe 3I/ATLAS multiple times in late 2025 as it drew closer to the Sun. On two separate observation dates, they measured methanol-to-hydrogen cyanide ratios of roughly 70 and 120, placing the comet among the most methanol-rich ever studied.[2][1]

"Observing 3I/ATLAS is like taking a fingerprint from another solar system," Roth said. "The details reveal what it's made of, and it's bursting with methanol in a way we just don't usually see in comets in our own solar system."[1]

items.title: Engineers hide data in heat radiation using 'negative light'

featured_image.name: New 'negative light' technology hides data transfers in ...

items.description: Engineers at UNSW Sydney and Monash University have built a communication system that conceals data transmissions within natural heat radiation, making them virtually undetectable. The technology, described in a paper published March 4 in the Nature Publishing Group journal Light: Science and Applications, exploits a phenomenon called "negative luminescence" to create what the researchers call "thermoradiative signatureless communication."[1][2]

items.title: Sydney researchers build AI chip that computes at speed of light

featured_image.name: Photonic chip that 'fits together like Lego' opens door to ...

items.description: Researchers at the University of Sydney have built a prototype artificial intelligence chip that processes data using light instead of electricity, performing calculations at the speed of light on a picosecond timescale — trillionths of a second. The nanophotonic chip, described in a study published in Nature Communications, points toward a future of faster and more energy-efficient AI hardware.[1][2]

items.title: Macron, IAEA chief open nuclear energy summit in Paris

featured_image.name: Macron to outline France's contribution to Europe's nuclear ...

items.description:
World leaders are convening in Paris on Monday for the second Nuclear Energy Summit, an event hosted by the French government in cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency to promote the expansion of civilian nuclear power at a moment of acute energy insecurity and escalating conflict in the Middle East.

French President Emmanuel Macron and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi opened the summit, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also delivering remarks. The gathering brings together heads of state and government, leaders of international organizations and financial institutions, and industry experts to discuss nuclear energy's role in decarbonization, energy security, and meeting surging electricity demand.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Oil's surge to $120 renews global push for clean energy

featured_image.name: Instant View: Oil surges 20% as Iran war fuels supply fears | Reuters

items.description:
The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, now entering its second week, has knocked out roughly a fifth of the world's oil and natural gas supply and sent energy prices surging — and the crisis is renewing calls from governments, investors, and analysts to accelerate the transition to domestically produced renewable energy.

Since the strikes began on February 28, Iran has retaliated by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, attacking energy infrastructure across the Persian Gulf, and forcing production stoppages from Qatar to Iraq. Brent crude has surged from about $73 before the conflict to around $120 on Monday, according to Reuters, rattling markets worldwide. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on its liquefied natural gas exports — representing about 20 percent of global LNG supply — after Iranian drone strikes, and may need at least a month to restore output.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Cortical Labs unveils data centers powered by human brain cells

featured_image.name: Human Brain Cells Run New Data Centers in Singapore ...

items.description: Australian biotech startup Cortical Labs announced Tuesday that it has unveiled the world's first biological data center in Melbourne and is building a second facility in Singapore, both powered not by conventional computer chips but by lab-grown human brain cells. The move represents a novel attempt to address the surging energy demands of artificial intelligence by turning to biology for computing power.

items.title: Oil nears $120 a barrel as Iran war sparks historic market surge

featured_image.name: Oil supertanker rates hit all-time high as Iran pledges to close the Strait of Hormuz

items.description: Oil prices surged past $100 a barrel on Monday for the first time since 2022, as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran entered its second week with no signs of abating. Brent crude briefly touched nearly $120 per barrel before settling around $105, marking what Reuters described as the benchmark's largest single-day gain ever in both percentage and absolute terms. The spike sent shockwaves through global financial markets, with Asian stocks plunging and European equities hitting their lowest levels in more than two months.[1][2]

items.title: Oil tops $100 a barrel as Iran war chokes global supply

featured_image.name: Oil prices surge, but no panic yet, as Iran war continues - NPR

items.description:
The price of crude oil surged past $100 a barrel on Monday as the U.S.-led war in Iran entered its second week, sending gasoline prices sharply higher for American consumers and raising fears of a prolonged energy crisis rooted in the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude climbed to $103.74 per barrel on March 9, up nearly 12% from the previous trading day alone and roughly 50% higher than a month ago, according to Trading Economics. WTI crude oil futures spiked as high as $108 per barrel after Sunday evening's futures open, a historic jump from $72 at the start of the prior week. The national average for a gallon of regular gasoline reached $3.47 on Monday, according to AAA, up from $2.99 just one week earlier — a rise of about 48 cents in seven days.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Iran fires drones at Saudi Arabia, Kuwait despite apology

featured_image.name: Saudi Arabia intercepts Iranian ballistic missiles, drones ...

items.description: Iran launched drones toward Saudi Arabia and Kuwait early Tuesday as the war engulfing the Middle East showed no signs of abating, with Gulf states continuing to intercept near-daily aerial attacks more than 10 days into the conflict. The Saudi Defense Ministry said it intercepted and destroyed two drones over the kingdom's oil-rich eastern region, while Kuwait's National Guard reported shooting down six drones targeting the country's northern and southern areas, according to the Associated Press.[1]

items.title: US rejects Iran's claim that warship sunk by torpedo was unarmed

featured_image.name: US submarine sinks Iranian warship off Sri Lanka killing at ...

items.description:
A U.S. Navy submarine torpedoed and sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena in the Indian Ocean on March 4, killing at least 84 sailors in what marked the first American submarine attack on an enemy warship since World War II. Five days later, Washington and Tehran are locked in a dispute over whether the vessel was armed when it was struck, as the incident widens the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict far beyond the Middle East.

The U.S. Indo-Pacific Command on Sunday rejected Iran's claim that the Dena was unarmed, calling the assertion "false" in a statement posted on X. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh had told reporters in New Delhi that the warship was "ceremonial" and "unarmed," saying it had been attending India's Milan 2026 naval exercise by invitation. An Indian Navy official, speaking anonymously, said the vessel was not "entirely unarmed".[1][2][3]

items.title: Kuwait's emir condemns Iran's 'brutal attack' in first address since strikes began

featured_image.name: Iran continues to strike Gulf infrastructure, hitting Kuwait ...

items.description:
Kuwait held military funerals on Monday for two interior ministry border security officers killed during ongoing Iranian strikes, as the country's leader broke his silence to condemn Tehran's assault on the Gulf state now entering its second week.

Lieutenant Colonel Abdullah Emad Al-Sharrah and Major Fahad Abdulaziz Al-Mejmed, both from the General Administration of Land Border Security, were buried at Sulaibikhat Cemetery in a ceremony led by First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef Al-Sabah. The Interior Ministry said the two men were "martyred at dawn" on Sunday but did not provide further details on the circumstances of their deaths.[1][2][3]

items.title: Iran rebuffs France's plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: Iran Threatens 'Severe' Response to US Sanctions Against Larijani

items.description: Iran's top security official dismissed France's plans to organize a naval mission to reopen the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, warning that no security arrangement can succeed while the war ignited by the United States and Israel continues to rage across the Middle East.

items.title: CENTCOM denies Patriot misfire, blames Iranian drone for Bahrain civilian injuries

featured_image.name: State Dept. clears $2.5 billion sale of Patriot missile ...

items.description: Competing narratives emerged on Monday over what caused damage to a residential neighborhood in Manama, Bahrain, with the United States and Iran offering sharply different accounts of an incident that injured dozens of civilians amid the ongoing military conflict in the region.

items.title: IAEA chief says Iran's enriched uranium likely survived strikes at Isfahan

featured_image.name: Meet IAEA chief Rafael Grossi: The man central to the Iran ...

items.description:
Nearly half of Iran's uranium enriched to 60% purity — just short of weapons-grade — appears to have survived months of military strikes, stored deep inside a tunnel complex at Isfahan that withstood the initial US-Israeli bombing campaign last June, the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog said Monday.

Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, told reporters in Paris that his agency believes "slightly more than 200 kg, possibly a bit more" of 60% enriched uranium was at Isfahan at the time of the last IAEA inspection before the June 2025 strikes. That material, he said, is probably still there.[1]

"The prevailing assumption is that the material remains there. We have not observed — and not just us, but generally all observers utilizing satellite imagery and other methods to monitor the facility — any signs of movement that would suggest the material has been transferred," Grossi said, according to Reuters.[1]
